# Export documents

::: {.doc-lead}
Choose a file format, apply a journal style, and check the result.
:::

## Export {#export}

The **Export** button in the status bar — or **Alt+E** — opens a dialog with two
independent choices: the **file format** (PDF, Word, HTML) and the **journal style**.
Every format saves where you choose, defaulting to the project's `exports/` — the
suggested file name follows the format you pick, so switching to Word gives you a `.docx`
name, not the `.pdf` one the dialog opened on (a name you choose yourself is kept). Word and
journal-styled PDF run through Quarto (the dialog says so when Quarto isn't installed —
see [Installation](/install/)); a long render shows its progress and can be
cancelled. Figure renders, captions, and panel references are all resolved during export,
and failures surface as a toast naming what to fix.

### Journal styles {#journal-styles}

Choosing a journal — **Nature**, say — makes the exported file follow that journal's house
style: how figure and panel references read (`Fig. 1a,b`), how citations are marked
(superscript numerals, before the punctuation), how reference entries are built (all
authors up to five, then `et al.`), what order the sections appear in, and the submission
formatting a manuscript needs (12pt Times, double-spaced, line-numbered).

**Your writing never changes.** The editor keeps Flux's own conventions no matter which
journal is selected — chips, figure references and caption leads look the same whether you
are aiming at Nature or nowhere. Only the exported file and the preview follow the journal,
so switching journals is instant, and switching back loses nothing. Nothing is rewritten in
your manuscript on disk: a journal style is a lens on the way out, not an edit.

Selecting a style is remembered per project, and agents can use the same one from the
terminal with `flux compile --to docx --style nature`.

### Journal Check {#journal-check}

**Alt+J** opens **Journal Check**, which reads your manuscript against the selected
journal's rulebook: title and summary-paragraph length, headings the journal doesn't print
(Nature uses neither "Introduction" nor "Results"), missing sections like Data availability,
word budgets, display-item and reference caps, and typed-out figure references that don't
match house style. Click any item to jump to it.

It is **advice, and never blocks an export** — Nature itself says style and length won't
influence consideration at first submission. Switch the panel to *Accepted / final* and the
sections a journal requires at acceptance become warnings rather than notes.

One deliberate limit: Flux formats references it owns — the ones you insert as figure
references — and only *points at* figure references you typed by hand. It cannot tell your
"Figure 2, panel D" from a mention of someone else's Figure 2D, so it never rewrites your
prose.

## PDF dependencies {#pdf-dependencies}

Flux's built-in PDF export needs neither Quarto nor TeX. Word and journal-styled exports use Quarto; Quarto PDF also needs TeX. **Set up Flux** can install Quarto and TinyTeX.

Journal styles may need additional TeX packages and an SVG converter:

| Environment | Additional packages |
|---|---|
| TinyTeX | `tlmgr install lineno setspace` |
| MacTeX | `sudo tlmgr install lineno setspace` |
| Debian / Ubuntu TeX Live | `sudo apt install texlive-latex-recommended texlive-humanities texlive-luatex texlive-fonts-recommended` |

Install `rsvg-convert` through `librsvg` on Homebrew or Arch, or `librsvg2-bin` on Debian/Ubuntu. Check it with `rsvg-convert --version`. TeX can locate a package with `kpsewhich lineno.sty setspace.sty`.

TinyTeX's own commands may need its bin folder on your shell's PATH: `~/Library/TinyTeX/bin/universal-darwin` on macOS or `~/.TinyTeX/bin/x86_64-linux` on Linux. Flux and Quarto can find TinyTeX without that shell change. These dependencies do not affect Word export.
